tool_summary: A shell builtin that concatenates its arguments and executes the result as shell code. One of the most direct arbitrary-code-execution primitives available, since the executed content can itself be dynamically constructed.
platform_notes: eval is a POSIX-required shell builtin, behavior consistent across sh/bash/zsh/dash. Because it is a builtin rather than a separate binary, it is typically only visible to commandant when it appears as an argument to a shell invocation (e.g. within a -c payload) rather than as a standalone command in isolation -- see the destructive-payload rules in sh.json/bash.json/etc.

rules.description: eval executes its argument as shell code after the shell's own expansion has already run. If the argument is built from variable content (command substitution, user input, a fetched string) rather than a fixed literal, the executed code is not fully knowable from the static command text.
rules.reversible_note: Reversibility depends entirely on the evaluated code, which may not even be fully visible in the static command string if it is dynamically constructed.
rules.notes: eval's argument may contain a literal, fully visible command (lower real risk despite the rule's flat ERROR severity) or a dynamically constructed one (the genuinely dangerous case). commandant cannot currently distinguish these without evaluating the shell expansion itself, so this rule treats all eval invocations uniformly as the worst case. See R-INS-05 for the general opaque-execution problem this shares with sudo/su/chroot.
